answer.rationale: Timing is the strongest signal available: the release landed ~2h ago and the write-path p99 climb began ~90m ago, so the release is the leading suspect and memory_b6 (staged/canary gating, often region-scoped) plausibly explains why the damage is confined to the primary region rather than global. That makes rollback_release the intervention most likely to remove the cause rather than mask it. I want to verify memory_b1 before committing because the consolidated summary says rollback cleared an 'error spike' — not a write-path latency creep — and it does not say whether it was done under peak write load or whether the release carried an irreversible data/schema migration; if the original record shows a low-traffic window or a no-migration build, its transfer to today is weak. I want memory_b2 verified because regional_failover is the obvious alternative given the degradation is region-confined, but shifting regions at settlement peak with heavy writes risks in-flight and replication-lagged writes — a direct hit to the 'do not lose customer writes' constraint — and I need to know whether the March degradation involved comparable write volume or was read-dominated before trusting 'traffic shifted cleanly.' Downstream value risk: failover and circuit-breaker both trade customer writes for latency optics; add_capacity (memory_b3) and route_read_replicas (memory_b5) address queue/read pressure and would likely mask a release regression while it keeps writing bad state, burning the single intervention. I am staging the rollback as a guarded canary cohort first so the causal link is confirmed on a small slice before broad application; if latency does not respond, the release is exonerated and failover becomes the next-window candidate. Uncertainty retained: none of these memories were recorded under simultaneous peak-write plus fresh-release conditions, so all are analogies, not precedents.
